subject: Cloud Computing
title: Data Gravity: Why Data is Hard to Move
description: A fast breakdown of Data Gravity: Why Data is Hard to Move for builders.

hook.text: Your data is in AWS. Moving 500 TB to Google Cloud would take months and cost a fortune in egress fees.

buildup.text: Data gravity means applications and services cluster around data. The bigger the dataset, the harder it is to move.

discovery.text: It's cheaper and faster to move compute to data than data to compute. Build your apps where your data already lives.

twist.text: Cloud providers know this. That's why ingress is free — getting data in is easy. Getting it out is the trap.

climax.text: Data gravity is the strongest force in cloud strategy. Where your data sits determines where everything else goes.

punchline.text: Data doesn't move easily. Everything else moves to the data.

quiz.question: Why do applications tend to cluster around data?
options: Moving large datasets is expensive and slow, so it's easier to move compute instead
Cloud providers only allow applications near their data centers
Applications cannot function more than 100 miles from their data

details.summary: Data gravity describes how large datasets attract applications, services, and more data to the same location. Moving petabytes of data between clouds or regions is slow, expensive, and risky. Applications tend to migrate toward data rather than the reverse.
details.whyItMatters: Data gravity is the hidden force behind cloud lock-in. Once data accumulates in one provider, the cost and difficulty of moving it makes switching providers practically impossible.
takeaways: Large datasets attract applications and services to their location
Moving petabytes is slow, expensive, and operationally risky
Data gravity is the primary driver of cloud vendor lock-in

faq.question: Why is data so expensive to move between clouds?
faq.answer: Cloud providers charge egress fees for data leaving their network. At petabyte scale, egress costs can reach hundreds of thousands of dollars. Physical transfer using devices like AWS Snowball takes weeks. Network transfer of petabytes can take months.

faq.question: How can organizations mitigate data gravity?
faq.answer: Use portable data formats and open standards. Maintain data catalogs that track where data lives. Consider multi-cloud data strategies early before data accumulates. Build abstraction layers that decouple applications from specific storage services.
